title: Individual care vs. community health
body: Individual care treats one person: an exam, a prescription, a shot.
Community health changes things everyone shares, like clean water, safe streets, or a clinic within walking distance.
A quick test: if the action helps many people who never walked into a doctor's office, it is community health.

steps.caption: One patient at a time
steps.art: A nurse helps each patient in turn: 1 person, 1 visit.

steps.caption: Change the shared setting
steps.art: Fix the water and every household is protected, even people who never see a doctor.

title: Products are not public health
body: Selling something is not the same as organized work to protect a group's health.
Public health uses data, planning, and shared resources to reduce risks across a population.

title: Choices live inside conditions
body: People do make choices, but choices depend on what is available.
If the only store nearby sells chips and soda, or no safe park exists, healthy options are harder.
Community health asks: what could we change so the healthy choice is the easy choice?

steps.caption: Same person, two places
steps.art: A neighborhood with a grocery store and park makes healthy habits easier.

steps.caption: Same effort, harder path
steps.art: A neighborhood without them makes the same effort much harder.

title: Genes are only part of the story
body: Genes affect health, but they cannot explain big differences between neighborhoods a few miles apart.
When families move to a place with different conditions, their health often changes over time.

title: Patterns are not chance
body: Chance can explain small, one-time differences.
When a gap is large and shows up year after year in the same places, something systematic is causing it.

title: From one person to a group
body: Clinical questions are about one patient: What is wrong? What treatment?
Population questions compare groups: Who is affected most? Why? What would help many people?

steps.caption: Zoom in
steps.art: A clinician looks at one person's chart.

steps.caption: Zoom out
steps.art: A health department looks at rates in every neighborhood.

title: Counting is not the same as comparing
body: A single count does not tell us about a population's health.
Population health compares rates between groups and asks why they differ.

title: Reservoir vs. vehicle
body: The reservoir is where the germ lives and multiplies: a person, an animal, or sometimes water or soil.
The vehicle is the thing that carries the germ to a new person: food, water, hands, a surface.
Think of the reservoir as the bus depot and the vehicle as the bus.

title: The host is the person
body: The susceptible host is the person who could get sick.
Food, water, and surfaces are never the host; they carry the germ.

title: Exit, route, entry
body: The germ has to leave the first person (portal of exit), travel (mode of transmission), and enter a new person (portal of entry).
Do not mix up leaving and entering: stool or vomit is how it leaves, swallowing is how it enters.

title: Where cases go missing
body: Most missing cases are not counting mistakes. They are people who never moved up the pyramid.
Illness, then seeking care, then a test, then a result, then a report. Each step loses people.

steps.caption: 50 reported
steps.art: Only these show up in the data.

title: Reports are the tip of the iceberg
body: Reported cases are only the visible tip.
Surveillance is built to spot trends and outbreaks, not to count every illness.

title: Why the latest days look low
body: Illness starts first. Then care, testing, and reporting take days.
So the newest days on a chart are incomplete and fill in later.

title: Too broad or too narrow?
body: Too broad: includes many people who are not cases (false positives). Specificity is low.
Too narrow: leaves out real cases (false negatives). Sensitivity is low.
Start broad to find cases, then tighten to study the cause.

steps.caption: Broad
steps.art: Everyone with any symptom: catches nearly all cases but also many colds.

steps.caption: Narrow
steps.art: Every symptom plus one place: few false cases but misses many real ones.

title: Balance beats extremes
body: A good definition catches most real cases and leaves out most non-cases.
Adding criteria lowers sensitivity; removing them lowers specificity.

title: Reading the shape
body: Point source: one narrow peak, because everyone was exposed at once.
Continuous source: a long plateau, because exposure keeps going.
Propagated: repeated waves, one incubation period apart, because each wave infects the next.

title: Counts vs. rates
body: A count says how many. A rate says what share of a group.
Attack rate = cases ÷ people at risk × 100.

title: Divide, do not subtract
body: Relative risk compares two attack rates by dividing: exposed ÷ unexposed.
A subtraction gives a risk difference, which is a different measure.

title: Which goes on top?
body: Exposed attack rate goes on top, unexposed on the bottom.
RR above 1: the exposure goes with more illness. RR near 1: little difference. RR below 1: protective.

title: Association is not proof
body: A high relative risk shows association, not cause.
Always ask whether something else could explain both the exposure and the illness.

title: The hidden third factor
body: A confounder is connected to both the exposure and the outcome.
To check, compare within groups of the possible confounder.

title: Compare with the baseline
body: An outbreak means more cases than expected for that place and time.
Every disease has a normal range. A jump far above it is a signal to look closer.

title: Evidence before sources
body: Names of suspects come after data.
First confirm the outbreak, define cases, and describe who, where, and when.

title: Small samples wobble
body: Different random samples can give different answers.
The smaller the sample, the larger the wobble.
A comparison group and more interviews narrow the guesswork.

title: Bias vs. other problems
body: Recall bias is about memory: sick people may remember more carefully, and everyone forgets over time.
Confounding is a third factor. Delay is about timing of data. Keep them separate.

title: Whose limitation is it?
body: Investigation limits come from the real-world process: underreporting, small samples, memory.
Model limits are what the simulation leaves out or simplifies.

title: Every study has limits
body: No dataset is perfect. Naming limits tells readers how much weight to give results.

title: A model is not the world
body: A model simplifies reality on purpose.
Naming what it leaves out is part of good science.

title: Share enough, protect people
body: People need information to protect themselves, but details about individuals can identify them, especially in small areas.
De-identify cases, use broader groupings, and share only what is needed.

title: Blame the source, not the people
body: Outbreaks come from places, foods, or conditions, not from a community's character.
Language that points at a neighborhood or group can cause stigma and discourage people from seeking care.

title: The world you can't see
body: You can only watch one version of events. The counterfactual is the one where you did nothing.
The difference between the two is the effect of your action.

steps.caption: Counterfactual
steps.art: What would have happened without it.

title: Problem first, solution later
body: Good community decisions follow steps: define the problem with data, identify who is affected, listen, consider options, weigh equity, decide, evaluate.
Jumping to a solution skips learning what the problem is and who it affects.

steps.caption: Define
steps.art: Use data to describe the problem.

title: More than the decision-makers
body: Stakeholders include anyone affected by a decision or able to influence it.
Ask who benefits, who bears costs, and who is left out.

title: Skeptics are stakeholders too
body: People who disagree often see risks that supporters miss.
Including them builds a stronger, fairer decision.

title: Barriers decide who shows up
body: Work schedules, childcare, language, transportation, and trust all affect who can take part.
If only the easiest people to reach are heard, the decision reflects only them.

steps.caption: Who is missing
steps.art: People working evenings or without a car.

steps.caption: Fix
steps.art: Go to them: weekend, local place, childcare, interpreters.

title: Don't study the page, study the source
body: Reading a post closely will not tell you whether to trust it.
Lateral reading: open new tabs and see what other reliable sources say.

steps.caption: Lateral
steps.art: Leave the post, search the claim and the source.

title: Popular is not true
body: Likes and shares measure attention, not accuracy.
Check the source, the evidence, and what independent sources say.

title: Trust drives belief
body: People act on information from people they trust.
Faith leaders, elders, coaches, and bilingual neighbors can make accurate facts believable.

title: Facts need a believable voice
body: Official facts matter, but they may not reach everyone.
Pair accurate information with someone the community already trusts and with the languages people use.

title: Gaps point to conditions
body: A large gap between places points to conditions such as air, housing, and access.
Blaming people hides what could change.

title: Compare rates
body: To judge a gap, divide one rate by the other.
17.8% against 6.5% is nearly three times as high.

title: Data and lived experience
body: Data show patterns across many people. Residents know what daily life is like.
When they disagree, treat the disagreement as a clue.

title: Voices need checking
body: Residents' experience is real evidence, and so are data.
Use both, and ask why they differ.

title: Luck and judgment
body: A good decision can have a bad outcome, and a bad decision can get lucky.
Judge the reasoning and information at the time, then learn from the result.

title: Opportunity cost
body: Opportunity cost is what you give up by choosing one option over the next best.
Ask what you lose, and who bears it.
